items.title: Ask to be put back on the roll with Form 6
items.plain: If your name was left off the draft or the final roll, fill in Form 6, the application to be added to the roll. During the claims and objections period of the revision it goes with the declaration attached to it for the revision. Once the revision is over in your state you can still apply at any time under continuous updation, on the ordinary Form 6 of the 1960 Rules. Form 6A is for Indian citizens living abroad, and Form 8 is for a change of address or a mistake in your own entry.
steps: Get Form 6 from your booth level officer (BLO), the registration officer's office, voters.eci.gov.in or the ECINet app.
During the revision, attach the declaration that goes with Form 6 for the revision.
Hand it to the BLO or the registration officer, or file it online, and keep the reference number.

Know what the ordinary Form 6 asks you to sign. It is titled “Application Form for New Voters”, and item (iii) of its declaration says “I am applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the first time and my name is not included in any Assembly Constituency/ Parliamentary Constituency.” The Commission's letter of 1 October 2026 tells booth level officers to help people who are no longer on the roll apply through Form 6, its Manual on Electoral Rolls of March 2023 says a person no longer on the roll has to apply again through Form 6 as a new elector, and section 23(1) of the 1950 Act lets anyone not on the roll apply. No Commission document found says how a person who was on a roll before should answer item (iii). Section 31 of the 1950 Act punishes only a statement the person knows or believes to be false, or does not believe to be true, with up to one year in prison, a fine or both, and no court ruling or prosecution for signing item (iii) to get back on the roll has been found.
Apply well before an election is called. No name can be added after the last date for nominations until that election is over.
Use Form 8 if you moved within the state or your entry has a mistake. Use Form 6A if you live abroad on an Indian passport.

items.title: Objections and the hearing before any deletion
items.plain: Form 7 is the form for objecting to a name on the roll, or to a name proposed to be added. Before a name is deleted for being dead, shifted or not entitled, the registration officer has to give notice and hold a hearing where the person objected to can appear. In the revision no entry could be deleted from the draft without an inquiry and a fair chance to be heard, followed by a written order with reasons. If you get a notice, go to the hearing or send the documents asked for, and ask for the order in writing.
steps: Check the lists of claims and objections the registration officer puts up on the notice board and the Chief Electoral Officer's website.
If someone has objected to your name, you should get a notice with the date, time and place of the hearing.
Attend in person or through someone you authorise where that is allowed, and take your documents.
Ask for the registration officer's decision in writing. You need it for an appeal.

items.title: Appeal to the District Magistrate, then to the Chief Electoral Officer
items.plain: If the registration officer's decision goes against you, you can appeal to the District Magistrate under section 24 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. If the District Magistrate's order also goes against you, a second appeal lies to the state's Chief Electoral Officer. The Commission's revision order kept both appeals and gave 30 days from the District Magistrate's order for the second. Chief Electoral Officers' notes on final rolls give 15 days from the registration officer's decision for the first.
steps: Get a copy of the registration officer's order.
Write a short appeal to the District Magistrate, signed by you, with the order attached, within 15 days.
If it is turned down, appeal to the Chief Electoral Officer within 30 days of the District Magistrate's order.
Keep copies and receipts of everything you hand in.

items.title: What the Supreme Court's orders give an elector
items.plain: In Bihar the Court had the roughly 65 lakh names left off the draft published booth by booth, with the reason for each, searchable by EPIC number and put up at panchayat and block offices. It allowed claims with a copy of Aadhaar and then made Aadhaar the twelfth document, as proof of identity. In West Bengal it let people flagged for discrepancies file through an authorised representative, gave them ten more days, and set up appellate tribunals of former judges for those whose claims judicial officers rejected. Its judgment of 27 May 2026 upheld the revision and said that people in Bihar whose names were, in its words, "erroneously deleted" as absent, dead, shifted or duplicate may challenge the decision in court.
steps: Search the list of names left off by your EPIC number on the district or Chief Electoral Officer's website, or look at the panchayat or block notice board.
Note the reason given against your name. It tells you what to answer.
Aadhaar can be given as proof of identity. It is not accepted as proof of citizenship.
In West Bengal, a rejected claim goes to the appellate tribunal. A pending appeal did not give a right to vote at the 2026 poll.

items.title: The 1950 helpline, complaints, and the drive to find those left off
items.plain: You can call the voter helpline on 1950, or the national toll-free number 1800-11-1950 from 8 am to 8 pm, and every complaint is logged on the National Grievance Service Portal. The ECINet app has a Book-a-Call with BLO feature, and complaints can also be emailed to complaints@eci.gov.in. After the revision, the Commission ordered BLOs to compare the roll from before the revision with the present one, visit those missing, and help anyone still eligible fill in Form 6. The lists are to be shared with the parties' booth agents, and camps are to be held, including for people in night shelters, labour colonies and the homeless.
steps: Call 1950, or 1800-11-1950, and note the complaint number.
Use Book-a-Call with BLO on the ECINet app to ask your BLO to visit.
If a BLO visits during the drive, fill in Form 6 then and there if you are eligible.
Look for booth level camps in your area, and special camps if you live in a night shelter or labour colony.

items.title: Free legal help from the legal services authorities
items.plain: Under section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, women, children, members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, people with disabilities, industrial workers, victims of disaster and people below an income limit set by each state can get free legal help. Legal services include advice and help before any authority, so they can cover a claim, a hearing or an appeal about the roll. Ask at the District Legal Services Authority at the district court, or call the NALSA helpline on 15100. In Bihar in September 2025 the Supreme Court had the legal services authorities send para-legal volunteers to help voters file claims and objections online.
steps: Call 15100 or visit the District Legal Services Authority office at the district court.
Say that your name was left off the roll and what stage you are at (claim, hearing or appeal).
Take the notice or order you received and any documents you have.
Ask for a para-legal volunteer or panel lawyer to help you fill in the form or the appeal.

items.title: Going to court
items.plain: An elector can ask the High Court, under Article 226 of the Constitution, to review a decision on the roll. The Supreme Court's judgment of 27 May 2026 says the Commission's enquiry into eligibility remains open to judicial review, and that people in Bihar whose names were, in its words, "erroneously deleted" as absent, dead, shifted or duplicate may challenge the decision that way. While the Supreme Court was hearing the challenge to the revision itself, it asked the High Courts on 11 November 2025 to hold back cases on whether the revision was valid. That request covered cases on whether the revision was valid, and the Supreme Court has since decided them.
steps: Use the claim, the hearing and both appeals first, and keep every order.
If you still have no remedy, ask the District Legal Services Authority for a lawyer to file a writ petition in the High Court.

sources.doc: Supreme Court judgment, ADR v. ECI, 2026 INSC 564, para 175
sources.quote: Importantly, the entirety of this exercise remains amenable to judicial review, thereby ensuring that the enquiry is conducted in accordance with law and within the bounds of procedural fairness.

sources.doc: Supreme Court order of 11.11.2025 in W.P.(C) No. 1074/2025, as reproduced in the Supreme Court registry office report for 26.11.2025
sources.quote: Since this Court is seized of the matter pertaining to validity of Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls in various States, including Bihar, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry etc., we request the jurisdictional High Courts to keep in abeyance/defer the writ proceedings, if any, filed in those High Courts touching the validity of the SIR of electoral rolls in their respective States.
sources.note: The order PDF itself was not found; the quote is from the registry office report, which reproduces it. The matters were disposed of by the judgment of 27.05.2026.

items.doc: Supreme Court judgment, ADR v. ECI, 2026 INSC 564, para 175
items.quote: Importantly, the entirety of this exercise remains amenable to judicial review, thereby ensuring that the enquiry is conducted in accordance with law and within the bounds of procedural fairness.

gaps: Article 226 of the Constitution was not quoted from a primary text fetched in this session; the writ item rests on the Supreme Court's own words about judicial review.

No Supreme Court order was found that bars High Courts from hearing an individual elector's case about his or her own entry. The 11.11.2025 request covers writs on the validity of the SIR only, and only the registry office report reproducing it was read.
The Supreme Court order of 01.09.2025 (para-legal volunteers in Bihar) was not found on api.sci.gov.in; it is cited through para 10.12 of the 27.05.2026 judgment.
The order of 09.10.2025 asking the Bihar SLSA to help excluded voters file appeals was found only in press reports (Verdictum, Deccan Herald), read through a summariser.

The current text of rule 27 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 (two-tier appeal, time limits) was not read. The copy on thc.nic.in predates the 2009 amendment of section 24 and still shows a single appeal to the CEO within fifteen days and a Rs 5 fee. The 15-day first appeal and 30-day second appeal come from the ECI SIR order and CEO Goa's press note.
India Code (indiacode.nic.in) timed out from the sandbox; the Act and Rules are cited from the High Court of Tripura's published copies, whose PDF text layer breaks some words.
Forms 6A and 8 could not be downloaded from voters.eci.gov.in (406) or voterportal.eci.gov.in (502); they are supported by rule 8B and rule 13(3) of the 1960 Rules and the CEO Karnataka note.
CEO Karnataka's press note of 24.08.2026 reset the connection on re-check on 2026-10-09; its quote was verified against the copy read earlier in this project.
The ECI Secretary's letter of 29.09.2026, to which the 01.10.2026 special-drive letter refers, was not found.

Press reported (LiveLaw, 05.10.2026) the Chief Justice saying a modified Form 6 had not been approved by the Supreme Court, against ECI PN/120's statement that the SIR declaration was upheld. No order was found. The Form 6 item states only what the ECI said.
No NALSA or SLSA scheme or circular specific to electoral roll cases in the SIR was found beyond the Bihar directions.
Rule 26(3)-(4) (seven-day notice on Form 6/7/8 applications outside a revision, and written reasons for rejection) was read but not used as a separate quote.
